title: Can You Retire on $1.5 Million and Live Comfortably?
metaDescription: Can you retire on $1.5 million comfortably? See what annual income it generates at 4% and 3.5%, how Social Security helps, and key budget factors.
h1: Can You Retire on $1.5 Million Comfortably?
cardBlurb: A $1.5 million nest egg generates $52,500 to $60,000 in baseline annual income before Social Security, creating a comfortable retirement for many households.
introText:
You can retire on $1.5 million comfortably if your planned annual household expenses fit within $52,500 to $60,000 of portfolio withdrawals plus your anticipated Social Security benefits.

At ModernWallet, we evaluate retirement cash flows by looking at withdrawal math and real household budgets rather than relying on abstract rules of thumb. The portfolio alone produces a predictable baseline of pre-tax cash flow, but your ultimate comfort depends on location, debt obligations, healthcare coverage, and when you begin taking government benefits.

Understanding how these pieces fit together lets you determine whether $1.5 million meets your personal retirement targets before you hand in your notice.

sections.heading: Annual Income Generated by $1.5 Million at Standard Withdrawal Rates
sections.body:
A $1.5 million portfolio provides between $52,500 and $60,000 in annual pre-tax retirement income under standard planning assumptions. The traditional benchmark for retirement planning is the 4% initial withdrawal rule, established by the [Trinity Study research](https://www.aaii.com/journal/article/retirement-savings-choosing-a-withdrawal-rate-that-is-sustainable) authored by Cooley, Hubbard, and Walz in 1998. At a 4% initial withdrawal rate, your $1.5 million portfolio supports $60,000 in annual distributions before income taxes.

Many financial planners recommend a slightly more conservative 3.5% initial withdrawal rate to provide an added cushion against market downturns or to accommodate a retirement horizon exceeding 30 years. At a 3.5% withdrawal rate, your $1.5 million savings balance generates $52,500 per year before taxes. In both approaches, you adjust your dollar withdrawal amount annually to keep pace with inflation.

These initial figures reflect only portfolio distributions and do not include other income sources. For most American workers, Social Security substantially increases spendable income. In 2026, the average monthly Social Security retirement benefit for a retired worker reached approximately $2,071, which equates to about $24,850 annually, following the 2.8% cost-of-living adjustment announced by the [Social Security Administration](https://www.ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html). When you combine an average Social Security benefit with a 4% portfolio withdrawal rate, your total gross household income reaches nearly $85,000 per year. For a married couple with two separate Social Security benefit histories, gross annual income can exceed $100,000.

sections.heading: Core Factors That Determine Personal Comfort in Retirement
sections.body:
Comfort in retirement depends on your fixed living expenses rather than portfolio size alone. Geographic location exerts the greatest influence on your baseline spending. A single person or couple with no dependents in a moderate or lower cost-of-living area finds that $60,000 in portfolio withdrawals plus Social Security stretches comfortably across daily living, leisure, and home maintenance. In contrast, running the same budget in an expensive metropolitan region leaves little room for discretionary spending because property taxes, utilities, and general services consume a larger share of cash flow.

Your housing situation plays an equally decisive role in determining comfort. Carrying a mortgage payment into retirement introduces a large mandatory monthly outflow that restricts your flexibility. Eliminating a mortgage before retiring reduces your required baseline income, which allows a $1.5 million balance to cover groceries, utilities, transportation, and travel with minimal financial stress.

Healthcare timing introduces another critical expense category. If you retire before turning age 65, you must fund your own private health insurance before becoming eligible to enroll through [Medicare](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/medicare-basics/how-do-i-get-medicare). Premiums and out-of-pocket deductibles for individual coverage can absorb thousands of dollars per year from your budget. Once you reach age 65, Medicare covers a substantial portion of medical care, though you still need to budget for supplemental policies, prescription plans, and dental care.

Tax diversification across your accounts also affects your real spendable income. Distributions from traditional 401(k) plans and individual retirement accounts are taxed as ordinary income at regular federal and state rates. Withdrawals from Roth accounts are generally tax-free, while money drawn from taxable brokerage accounts faces capital gains tax rates on realized profits. Two retirees with identical $1.5 million balances can experience noticeably different net take-home incomes depending on the account types holding their assets.

sections.heading: Sizing Your Personal Spending against Portfolio Income
sections.body:
Determining whether $1.5 million is sufficient requires benchmarking your documented personal expenses against the $52,500 to $60,000 baseline range. Rather than relying on broad national spending averages that blend disparate lifestyles, review your actual bank and credit card statements from the past 12 to 24 months. Categorize your recurring obligations into essential costs and discretionary desires.

Essential costs include housing, groceries, insurance, utilities, property taxes, transportation, and baseline medical care. If your essential living expenses total $45,000 per year, a $1.5 million portfolio withdrawing 3.5% covers all basic needs even before counting Social Security benefits. In that scenario, every dollar of future Social Security income functions as pure discretionary buffer for hobbies, travel, and unexpected home repairs.

If your recurring essential expenses exceed $70,000 annually, a $1.5 million portfolio cannot support your lifestyle on its own without relying on sizable guaranteed pension or Social Security benefits. You can test your spending against portfolio distributions using our [retirement income calculator](/retirement/retirement-income-calculator/) to see your specific cash flow picture. You can also analyze your ongoing spending patterns with our [budget calculator](/budget/) to identify where your outflows go.

sections.heading: Portfolio Longevity across Different Withdrawal Rates and Horizons
sections.body:
The duration of your retirement portfolio depends heavily on your chosen withdrawal rate and the length of your retirement horizon. The classic 4% rule originated from empirical simulations covering historical 30-year retirement windows. For a retiree leaving the workforce at age 65, a 30-year horizon covers living expenses through age 95, a timeframe that fits standard actuarial life expectancies.

When planning for a longer horizon, such as retiring in your 50s, a 30-year model leaves potential gaps. Early retirees face horizons spanning 40 or 50 years, which increases exposure to economic cycles and inflation. In these extended timelines, reducing the initial distribution rate to 3.5% or 3.25% significantly improves portfolio durability, as we discuss in our analysis of whether [3 million is enough to retire at 40](/guides/is-3-million-enough-to-retire-at-40/).

Market sequence represents another primary threat to portfolio longevity. Sequence-of-returns risk occurs when severe stock market downturns happen in the initial years of your retirement, right when your portfolio balance is at its peak and you are actively taking distributions. Selling equities at depressed prices locks in portfolio losses and permanently diminishes the asset base available to compound when markets eventually recover. A prolonged market slump occurring late in retirement causes far less damage to overall solvency than one occurring in your first three years of withdrawals.

sections.heading: Strategies to Extend a $1.5 Million Retirement Fund
sections.body:
You can strengthen the safety margin of a $1.5 million portfolio by implementing several proven financial adjustments. The first method involves maintaining one to two years of living expenses in cash or short-term liquid reserves. Holding this cash buffer protects you from forced asset sales during equity downturns, allowing your investments time to rebound without interrupting your monthly income distributions.

Delaying Social Security is another lever that meaningfully extends the plan. While you can claim benefits starting at age 62, delaying your claim beyond your full retirement age earns delayed retirement credits. According to the [Social Security Administration rules on delayed retirement](https://www.ssa.gov/benefits/retirement/planner/agereduction.html), each year of delay between your full retirement age and age 70 increases your monthly benefit by approximately 8%. Delaying claims locks in a larger permanent, inflation-adjusted income stream that reduces the withdrawal burden placed on your investment accounts in later decades. You can model different claiming dates with our [Social Security retirement calculator](/retirement/social-security-retirement-calculator/).

Preserving growth potential inside your asset allocation is equally important for long-term purchasing power. Over a 25 to 30 year retirement horizon, inflation erodes fixed-dollar cash piles. Shifting an entire $1.5 million portfolio into cash or short-term certificates of deposit protects nominal balance stability but guarantees a loss of real purchasing power. Maintaining a disciplined allocation to broad-market equities provides the compounding necessary to offset rising prices for goods and services.

Finally, relocating to an area with lower property taxes and everyday living costs instantly expands your financial flexibility. Moving from a high-tax jurisdiction to a lower-cost region can reduce your annual budget by $10,000 to $20,000, allowing you to lower your portfolio withdrawal rate from 4% down to 3.2% while enjoying the same standard of living.

sections.heading: Scenarios Where $1.5 Million Falls Short and Key Countermeasures
sections.body:
A $1.5 million nest egg is not universally comfortable for every household profile. This balance falls short for households living in high-cost coastal metropolitan areas who still carry significant mortgage debt, support college-age dependents, or face extensive private healthcare costs before reaching Medicare eligibility at age 65. If your mandatory recurring obligations total $85,000 annually without outside pension income, withdrawing that sum from a $1.5 million portfolio requires an initial withdrawal rate of 5.67%. That withdrawal rate creates severe depletion risk over a typical 30-year horizon.

Specific financial conditions can shift this verdict favorably. If you enter retirement with a completely paid-off primary residence, your monthly housing expenditure drops to property taxes, insurance, and routine upkeep. That reduction alone can trim $20,000 to $30,000 from annual baseline expenses, bringing a demanding budget back into the safe 3.5% to 4% distribution range.

Similarly, entering retirement with Social Security benefits already active immediately lowers portfolio strain. If two spouses receive combined Social Security payments of $45,000 annually, they need only $35,000 from their investments to hit an $80,000 annual spending target. Drawing $35,000 from a $1.5 million portfolio represents a conservative 2.33% withdrawal rate, providing exceptional long-term financial security. If you want to evaluate alternative nest egg benchmarks, explore our guides on [how to retire with 1 million](/guides/how-to-retire-with-1-million/) and [how much you need to retire by age](/guides/how-much-do-i-need-to-retire-by-age/). To determine your personal timeline, calculate your exact target using our [FIRE calculator](/retirement/fire-calculator/) today.

faqs.question: Is $1.5 million enough to retire comfortably?
faqs.answer: Yes, $1.5 million is enough for many households to retire comfortably, supporting between $52,500 and $60,000 in annual pre-tax portfolio withdrawals under standard 3.5% to 4% rules. When combined with average Social Security benefits, gross household income often ranges between $77,000 and $100,000 or more, which easily covers comfortable living in moderate-cost areas.

faqs.question: How much income does $1.5 million generate in retirement?
faqs.answer: At a standard 4% initial withdrawal rate, a $1.5 million portfolio generates $60,000 per year before taxes. At a more conservative 3.5% withdrawal rate designed for extra safety or longer horizons, it produces $52,500 annually before taxes, with withdrawals adjusted each year for inflation.

faqs.question: Does Social Security count toward whether $1.5 million is enough?
faqs.answer: Yes, Social Security counts directly toward your retirement spending capacity and significantly reduces the withdrawal burden placed on your portfolio. In 2026, the average retired worker benefit is roughly $2,071 per month (about $24,850 per year), providing guaranteed income that layers on top of your investment distributions.

faqs.question: What withdrawal rate should I use for $1.5 million?
faqs.answer: A withdrawal rate of 3.5% to 4% is standard for a 30-year retirement horizon based on historical market research. If you retire early or want greater protection against sequence-of-returns risk, choosing a 3% to 3.5% rate provides greater portfolio longevity.

faqs.question: How can I make $1.5 million last longer in retirement?
faqs.answer: You can make $1.5 million last longer by delaying Social Security to age 70 to earn delayed retirement credits of roughly 8% per year, holding one to two years of spending in cash reserves to manage sequence risk, keeping moderate equity exposure to outpace inflation, and lowering fixed housing costs.
